scenario_prompt: Write a two-paragraph executive summary addressed directly to a fictional buyer's Chief Financial Officer, recommending a cloud migration. Context: a mid-market freight brokerage firm is moving its load-matching and carrier-settlement systems off on-premises Microsoft SQL Server (28 instances) running on Hyper-V (620 virtual machines) onto Google Cloud, targeting Google Compute Engine for compute and Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL for the data layer, over a 2-year, $4,200,000 programme. The CFO has stated she is measured on reducing the current $1,850,000 annual technology spend and on a clean DOT compliance audit, which opens in 6 months. Cover why this matters to her now and what she should expect from the programme. Return only the summary text, two paragraphs, no headers.
text:
Dear CFO,

Your current $1,850,000 annual technology spend is anchored by 28 on-premises SQL Server instances and 620 Hyper-V virtual machines that carry the fixed costs of licensing, hardware refresh cycles, and facilities regardless of actual load volumes — costs that don't flex with freight demand and won't shrink on their own. Migrating load-matching and carrier-settlement systems to Google Compute Engine and Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL over this two-year, $4,200,000 programme converts that fixed infrastructure burden into consumption-based spend, eliminates the recurring capital cycle of refreshing on-prem hardware, and removes SQL Server licensing as a line item entirely. You should expect the programme to pay back against your reduction target within the following 12–18 months post-cutover, with year-one spend elevated by parallel-running both environments before decommissioning realizes the savings — plan your budget narrative accordingly rather than expecting first-year relief.

The more immediate pressure is your DOT compliance audit opening in six months, and the migration timeline needs to be sequenced deliberately around it: carrier-settlement data — the system most likely to be in scope for audit evidentiary requests — should be prioritized early in the migration waves so it's stable on Cloud SQL well ahead of the audit window, not mid-cutover when auditors ask for records. Google Cloud's audit logging, IAM access controls, and data residency configuration give you a stronger compliance evidence trail than your current Hyper-V environment, but only if configured and validated before the audit opens, not during it. I recommend treating the audit date as the hard constraint that governs sequencing, with the cost-reduction case built around a realistic post-migration run rate rather than assumed savings during the transition — this protects you from being caught mid-migration with degraded audit readiness or an unexpected cost bump in either KPI you're measured on.
